nodes.label: Adjective Comparison (-ij- suffix / consonant softening)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 11's central topic: comparative degree formed either by -ij- suffix (most adjectives) or by softening the stem-final consonant (k→č, g→ž, h→š, t→ć, d→đ, etc.), the same softening set used for passive participles and verbal nouns. Superlative always prefixes naj- to the comparative. A handful of adjectives (dobar/bolji, loš/gori) are fully suppletive.

nodes.label: Verbal Aspect (Perfective/Imperfective)
nodes.rationale: Introduced Lesson 2, elaborated through Lesson 10: most BCS verbal ideas have two corresponding verbs sharing a root but differing in aspect — perfective (single completed action) vs. imperfective (repeated/ongoing/general). Aspect pairs form by prefixation or by suffixation (which often also shifts conjugation type, stem consonant/vowel). A pervasive grammatical mechanism referenced in nearly every lesson's grammar points.

nodes.label: B/C/S Dialect-Tag Convention ([B]/[C]/[S])
nodes.rationale: The Alexander & Elias-Bursać textbook's own boxed convention (p.23 of Lesson 2, restated across lessons): bracket tags after a word signal either (a) a pan-BCS form with a more-restricted regional alternate, or (b) a genuine lexical split where different standards prefer different words. Lesson 9's grammar note explicitly frames this as a simplification of a frequency gradient rather than a hard categorical split. Central organizing device for the whole textbook and for this project's Attested Region/Usage Tier tagging.

nodes.label: Clitic Second-Position / Ordering Rule
nodes.rationale: BCS clitics (short pronoun forms, the reflexive se, short 'to be' forms, the question particle li, and the future auxiliary) must occupy the clause's strict second position, in a fixed relative order (li - aux - dat - acc/gen - se - je). First introduced Lesson 1 (se-verb second-position rule), formalized in Lesson 6 and Lesson 10 with the full six-slot ordering.

nodes.label: Consonant Softening (Palatalization Set)
nodes.rationale: A recurring phonological alternation (k→č, g→ž, h→š, t→ć, d→đ, p→plj, b→blj, v→vlj, m→mlj, and k/g/h→c/z/s before certain endings) that resurfaces across multiple independent grammatical contexts: nominative plural, locative/dative singular, vocative case, passive participles, verbal nouns, feminine instrumental singular, and comparative adjectives.

nodes.label: Ekavian/Ijekavian Jat-Reflex Split ([E]/[J])
nodes.rationale: Common Slavic jat reflects as 'ije'(long)/'je'(short) in ijekavian (Bosnia, Croatia, southwestern Serbia, Montenegro) vs. 'e' in ekavian (most of Serbia). Attested independently by both the Magner and Alexander&Elias-Bursać textbooks starting at Lesson 1, and cuts across the B/C/S national-standard split rather than mapping one-to-one onto it (Serbian speakers can be either ekavian or ijekavian depending on region).

nodes.label: Future Tense (clitic ću/ćeš/će auxiliary)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 9's central grammar topic: future is a compound tense built from an auxiliary (clitic ću/ćeš/će... or full hoću/hoćeš/hoće, historically 'to want') plus the infinitive or da+present. Croatian/Serbian spelling and word-order conventions diverge (učit ću vs. učiću).

nodes.label: Genitive Case (formation and uses)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 4's central case topic: genitive follows most prepositions (treated as the 'default' case to memorize exceptions against), marks possession/of-relations, is required after invariant nema ('there is no...'), and expresses partitive direct objects (some of vs. the whole).

nodes.label: Instrumental Case (means, accompaniment, time)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 7's central case topic: instrumental (without preposition) expresses means/tool and means of transport; with s/sa expresses accompaniment; with pred/nad/za expresses spatial location; instrumental plural + already + present marks long-duration-still-continuing.

nodes.label: Locative/Dative Case Syncretism
nodes.rationale: Lesson 6's central topic: the dative singular has exactly the same forms as the locative singular (including the same k/g/h to c/z/s stem shift). Locative appears only after prepositions, tracking a fixed 'u-word'/'na-word' identity per noun. Dative marks indirect objects and the dative-experiencer construction for states/feelings (dosadno mu je 'he's bored').

nodes.label: Passive Participles (-n/-t/-en)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 11 grammar point: adjective-like forms describing completed actions, formed by adding -n (infinitive stem, most -ati verbs), -t (infinitive stem, types 7/11), or -en (present stem, sometimes with consonant softening) plus adjectival endings.

nodes.label: Past Tense (L-Participle + biti auxiliary)
nodes.rationale: Introduced Lesson 6, formalized fully in Lesson 10: past tense = present-tense auxiliary (clitic form of biti) + L-participle (named for its -l- marker), agreeing with the subject in gender/number. Governed by the fixed 6-slot clitic ordering rule and the 'je-final' rule for the 3sg auxiliary.

nodes.label: Gendered Profession Nouns (STRUKE table, B/C/S variation)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 11's STRUKE vocabulary table systematically pairs male/general and female forms for dozens of professions, with heavy B/C/S lexical divergence (kèmičar/hèmičar, liječnik/lèkar, pjesnik/pesnik, znànstvenik/nàučnik) and productive female-agentive suffix patterns (-ica, -ka, -kinja) — directly relevant to the project's future word-formation/slang-mechanics analysis given Alexander's Grammar Ch.18 finding that diminutive/agentive suffixes are the productive, affect-loaded categories.
nodes.norm_label: gendered profession nouns (struke table, b/c/s variation)

nodes.label: The Particle se (reflexive/reciprocal/passive/inclinational)
nodes.rationale: se marks at least seven distinct functions across the textbook: true reflexive, reciprocal ('each other'), impersonal, inclinational (feeling like doing something, person in dative), intransitive, non-causative, and passive. Some verbs never occur without se at all. Assembled across Lessons 1, 6, 8, and 9.

nodes.label: Subjectless / Dative-Experiencer Sentences
nodes.rationale: BCS sentences can lack a grammatical subject entirely, or carry a 'logical subject' in dative (feelings/states: dosadno mu je), genitive (quantity: mnogo ih ima), or accusative (emotions: strah me je 'I am afraid') case, always taking 3sg verb/neuter L-participle. Formalized Lesson 10, exemplified via inclinational se-verbs (sviđati se, dopadati se) from Lesson 6.

nodes.label: 16 Verb Conjugation Types
nodes.rationale: Lesson 10 formalizes the full 16-type conjugation-class system BCS verbs are grouped into by the infinitive-to-present-stem relationship (type 1 = a-conjugation; types 2-4 = i-conjugation; remaining types = e-conjugation), needed to predict past-tense L-participle formation and aspect-pair suffixation patterns used throughout the textbook.

nodes.label: Verbs of Transport (nos-/vod-/voz- root distinction)
nodes.rationale: BCS distinguishes three near-rhyming imperfective roots for 'take/carry [somewhere]' by what is being moved: nos- (inanimate object or a being that must be carried), vod- (a being moving under its own power on foot), voz- (a being moved by vehicle) — each with its own perfective partner and root shift. Introduced Lesson 7, extended with prefixed pairs in Lesson 10.

nodes.label: hleb / kruh / hljeb ("bread", three-way national split)
nodes.rationale: A clean three-way national lexical split for a basic everyday noun — hleb [S], kruh [C], hljeb [B] — recurring across Lesson 4's A3 vocabulary box and Lesson 6's C3 food-matching set, illustrative of genuine B/C/S vocabulary divergence rather than mere pronunciation variance.
nodes.norm_label: hleb / kruh / hljeb ("bread", three-way national split)

nodes.label: màslac / pùter ("butter", B,C,S vs B,S dialect pair)
nodes.rationale: Illustrative example of the pan-BCS-vs-restricted-alternate tagging pattern ([B,C,S] main form coexisting with a [B,S]-only synonym) captured across the textbook's food vocabulary in Lesson 7.
nodes.norm_label: maslac / puter ("butter", b,c,s vs b,s dialect pair)

nodes.label: nàrandža / nàranča / pomòrandža ("orange", three-way national split)
nodes.rationale: Second clean three-way national split (Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian) for a basic fruit noun, recurring across Lessons 4, 5, and 6 — repeatedly cited by this project's own extraction notes as a canonical illustration of full three-way lexical divergence.
nodes.norm_label: narandza / naranca / pomorandza ("orange", three-way national split)

nodes.label: "Ma moj!" Slang Retort (source-labeled slang)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 7's grammar section explicitly flags this as slang under the heading 'Amusing slang usage': there is no grammatical affirmative counterpart to the negative imperative nèmoj ('don't'), yet B/C/S colloquial usage has produced the ungrammatical-but-popular retort 'Ma moj!'/'Ma da moj!' in response to 'Ma nèmoj!', paralleling English 'No way!' → 'Way!'. First source-self-labeled slang item in this project.
nodes.community_name: Early Source-Labeled Slang & Project Index Docs

nodes.label: Teen/Regional Slang Family-Address Terms (kèva, stara/stari/starci)
nodes.rationale: Lesson 9's cultural-note vocabulary explicitly flags regionally-restricted colloquial father/mother terms (bàbo/nàna in Bosnia, ćaća/papo in Dalmatia, japa near Zagreb, ćàle in Belgrade) and labels kèva 'slang for mother' in Belgrade. Also documents a pan-regional teenage register: stara/stari/starci ('old woman'/'old man'/'oldsters') for mother/father/parents — the project's first explicit source-labeled slang register, alongside Lesson 7's 'Ma moj!' retort.
